title: Savvas MyView Illustrates The HQIM Farce
author: Daniel OK-Carr
summary: In a column republished by the Curriculum Insight Project, teacher Daniel OK-Carr argues that the HQIM label gives a false assurance of quality, using the 2025 "Science of Reading" version of Savvas MyView as his case. He bought the 2020 student textbook and found that the revamp mostly reordered worksheets, leaving stories, questions and close-read prompts unchanged. He challenges the "knowledge building" badge by describing units whose texts range from Martian microbiology to Angel Island interrogations, comparing them to a random pile of library books with a thematic label. He then walks through a week of teaching, where the first text mislabels leaf arrangements as a non-pattern, gets moth and butterfly development wrong and misdescribes pattern rules. His conclusion is that approval by gatekeepers such as EdReports does not guarantee a coherent, accurate or teachable curriculum.
points: The HQIM stamp implies research-backed rigor, but a revised program can change little beyond worksheet order and graphic design.
Thematic units that bundle unrelated texts under a broad theme call into question what "knowledge building" means in rubric reviews.
Building real knowledge from the program required hours of unpaid teacher time, outside books and a stretched pacing guide.
Basic factual and mathematical errors in a flagship text raise doubts about quality control at publishers and about the reviews that approve them.
quotes: That title should tell purchasers that what they bought is research-backed, rigorous, and aligned with how humans learn to read.
I bought the 2020 student textbook for my grade level to see the differences myself. What changed? I kid you not, the order of the worksheets.

Under this definition of knowledge building, I am reasonably confident I could go into my school library, randomly grab five different books from various genres, concoct some creative thematic connection, and call it a unit.

But to do this I had to dedicate hours upon hours of personal time, raid the library storage room for class sets of books (the 3rd through 5th grade core curriculum has students read 0 whole books over 3 years as a class), and generally apply a liberal interpretation of our 4th grade pacing guide.

Yet themes broad enough to encompass Martian astrobiology and the Chinese Exclusion Act make one question both Savvas’ commitment to building robust knowledge in students and the quality of EdReport evaluations.

If a curriculum claims to build background knowledge through “complex informational text”, at minimum that text should be scientifically and mathematically accurate. Somehow, in the very first text, it failed on both accounts.
Again 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 is not a pattern rule, and ladybugs have four wings, not two.
Those examples aren’t aberrations. Indeed, this degree of topical whiplash is present throughout the curriculum.
